title: Chapter 3.  History — The Anglo-Manipur War & Colonial Period

blocks.content: The Anglo-Manipur War of 1891 is Manipur's single most important modern-history event before Independence - a short but fiercely fought conflict that ended Manipuri sovereign independence and brought the kingdom under direct British political control, while also producing one of North-East India's most celebrated instances of armed resistance to colonial rule.

Political instability within the Manipuri royal court - specifically a palace coup in 1890 in which Senapati (military commander) Tikendrajit Singh and his allies deposed the reigning Maharaja in favour of a different prince - prompted British political intervention, since the British (who maintained a Resident/Political Agent at the Manipuri court as part of their protected-state relationship established after 1826) sought to arrest Tikendrajit and reassert control over the succession.

When a British military force arrived at Imphal in March 1891 to arrest Tikendrajit, Manipuri forces resisted, resulting in the deaths of several British political and military officers (including the Chief Commissioner of Assam, James Wallace Quinton) in what became known as the Imphal massacre/incident of 24 March 1891 - a pivotal event that triggered a full British military campaign against the kingdom.

The subsequent Anglo-Manipur War (1891) saw the British launch a punitive military expedition that defeated Manipuri forces within a matter of weeks; the kingdom's key military and political leaders - including Tikendrajit Singh and General/Commander Thangal General (Yumnam Thangal) - were captured, tried, and publicly hanged at Imphal in August 1891, an event still commemorated annually in Manipur as a significant date of anti-colonial martyrdom.

Following the war, the British formally reorganised Manipur's status: while nominally retaining the Manipuri monarchy under a new, British-approved ruler, the kingdom was brought under substantially tighter British political control, with the Manipur State Durbar administering the territory under close British Political Agent oversight for the remainder of the colonial period.

cells: Palace coup; Tikendrajit and allies depose the Maharaja
British force arrives at Imphal to arrest Tikendrajit; Imphal incident/massacre (Quinton and other officers killed)
Anglo-Manipur War; British punitive expedition defeats Manipuri forces
Tikendrajit Singh and Thangal General publicly hanged at Imphal

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: 13 August is commemorated in Manipur as 'Patriots' Day' (Deshbhakti Divas), honouring Tikendrajit Singh, Thangal General and other martyrs of the 1891 Anglo-Manipur War - a frequently tested date-and-commemoration fact, distinct from Manipur's later Statehood Day (Chapter 4).

items: Under British political oversight following 1891, Manipur retained a nominal monarchy but functioned effectively as a British-protected princely state, with the Manipur State Durbar (a council of the Maharaja and senior officials, closely supervised by the British Political Agent) managing day-to-day administration.

This arrangement continued through the remainder of British rule in India, including through the Second World War, during which Manipur (particularly Imphal) became a major theatre of fighting - the decisive Battle of Imphal (1944), fought alongside the Battle of Kohima in neighbouring Nagaland, halted the Japanese Army's attempted invasion of India and is widely regarded by military historians as one of the turning points of the South-East Asian theatre of World War II.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: The Battle of Imphal (1944), fought alongside the Battle of Kohima, halted the Japanese invasion of India during World War II and is frequently cited by military historians (including in a well-known National Army Museum, UK poll) as among 'Britain's Greatest Battles' - an important WWII-history crossover fact for Manipur.

items: Anglo-Manipur War (1891): triggered by the 1890 palace coup involving Senapati Tikendrajit Singh; British force killed at Imphal, 24 March 1891.
Tikendrajit Singh and Thangal General publicly hanged, 13 August 1891 - commemorated annually as Patriots' Day (Deshbhakti Divas).
Post-1891: Manipur retained a nominal monarchy under closer British political control via the Manipur State Durbar.
Battle of Imphal (1944, alongside the Battle of Kohima) halted the Japanese WWII invasion of India - a major turning-point battle of the South-East Asian theatre.
